```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H")

```
```{r data, include=FALSE}
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%
# Descriptive statistics
str(data)                                                    # variable types: 3 numeric, 10 factors
summary(data)                                                # numeric: min, quartiles, mean, max; factors: counts
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Churn)), 1)                # churn rate in %
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Contract)), 1)             # contract types in %
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Contract, data$Churn), 1), 1)        # churn rate per contract type
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$InternetService, data$Churn), 1), 1) # churn rate per internet service
```
```{r data split, include=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]
```
```{r grow tree, include=FALSE}
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)
```
```{r tune tree, include=FALSE}
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]
```
```{r prune tree, include=FALSE}
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %
```
```{r predictions test set, include=FALSE}
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")

conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

precision <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix["Yes", ]) # predicted churners that really churn
recall    <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # actual churners that are detected
f1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)          # harmonic mean of precision and recall
precision; recall; f1

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

```

# 1. Introduction

Since acquiring a new customer costs more than retaining an existing one, and customers become more profitable the longer they stay (Gupta et al., 2006), it is in a company's best interest to minimise churn, i.e. customers ending their contract and switching to a competitor. This report therefore investigates the churn behaviour of `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` customers of a telecom provider to gain insight into the factors that play a role in their decision to leave, addressing the question: **which customer characteristics are related to churn, and which customers should a telecom provider target to reduce it?**

# 2. Data

The data were provided by a telecom provider and contain `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` customers. For each customer, the data contain *Churn* (yes/no; `r format(sum(data$Churn == "Yes"), big.mark = ",")` or `r pct(churn_rate)` churned) and twelve predictors without missing values: the contract term (*Contract*; `r pct(mean(data$Contract == "Month-to-month"))` month-to-month), months with the company (*tenure*; median `r median(data$tenure)`), the monthly and total amount charged (*MonthlyCharges*, median \$`r round(median(data$MonthlyCharges))`; *TotalCharges*), whether the customer has a partner, phone service or multiple lines, the internet provider (*InternetService*: DSL, fibre optic or none) and four add-ons (online security, online backup, device protection, tech support). Churn differs strongly between groups: `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$Contract == "Month-to-month"] == "Yes"))` of month-to-month customers churned against `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$Contract == "Two year"] == "Yes"))` of two-year customers, and `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$InternetService == "Fiber optic"] == "Yes"))` of fibre customers against `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$InternetService == "DSL"] == "Yes"))` of DSL customers. The data are randomly split into a training set of `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` (70%) and a test set of `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` customers (30%), stratified by *Churn* so both sets have the same churn rate of `r pct(mean(test$Churn == "Yes"))`. Always predicting "no churn" thus gives a baseline accuracy of `r pct(acc_baseline)`.

# 3. Methods

To identify which characteristics are related to churn, a decision tree is used. Since churn is categorical, CART (Classification And Regression Trees; Breiman et al., 1984) builds a *classification tree*, which predicts the outcome through a series of yes/no questions, such as "is $X_1$ below 10?". Each question splits the observations into two more homogeneous groups; the final groups (*leaves*) predict their most common class, giving easy-to-read if-then rules (Yildirim & Kübler, 2023). Formally, each observation has a response $Y$ in one of $K$ classes and $p$ predictors $X_1, \dots, X_p$. The tree is built in five steps.

*First*, the tree is grown on a training set by *recursive binary splitting* (James et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2014). At each node $m$, every predictor $X_j$ and cut-point $s$ is tried. Each candidate splits the node into $\{X_j < s\}$ and $\{X_j \geq s\}$. The split with the lowest weighted Gini impurity of the two new nodes is chosen, where
$$G_m = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk}^2$$
and $\hat p_{mk}$ is the share of training observations in node $m$ that belong to class $k$. A pure node has $G_m = 0$. In a leaf, $\hat p_{mk}$ is the predicted probability of class $k$.

*Second*, because a fully grown tree also fits noise and this often leads to overfitting, it is *pruned* (Tan et al., 2014). In `rpart` (Therneau & Atkinson, 2023), the pruned tree is the subtree $T$ that minimises
$$R_{cp}(T) = R(T) + cp \cdot |T| \cdot R(T_0),$$
where $R(T)$ is the share of misclassified training observations, $|T|$ the number of leaves of $T$, $R(T_0)$ the misclassification rate of the tree without splits, and $cp \geq 0$ the **complexity parameter**. A split is only kept if it lowers the relative error by at least $cp$, so a larger $cp$ gives a smaller tree.

*Third*, $cp$ is chosen by **10-fold cross-validation** (James et al., 2013). The training set is divided into 10 parts and the tree is fitted on 9 parts. It is then tested on the remaining part, in turn. This gives a *cross-validated error* and its standard error; lower is better. The **one-standard-error rule** selects the smallest tree whose error is within one standard error of the minimum (Hastie et al., 2009).

*Fourth*, the selected tree is evaluated on a separate test set by its **accuracy** (share of correct predictions), **precision** $P$ (share of predicted positives that are correct), **recall** $R$ (share of actual positives detected) and **F1 score** $F_1 = 2PR/(P+R)$ (Tan et al., 2014). Higher is better; accuracy should clearly exceed the **baseline accuracy** of always predicting the majority class. *Finally*, a predictor's **variable importance** is its share of the total Gini reduction; higher is more important (de Oña et al., 2016).

# 4. Results

The full tree has `r max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])` splits; the cross-validated error is lowest (`r sprintf("%.3f", row_min["xerror"])`) at `r row_min["nsplit"]` splits. The one-standard-error rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp_1se)`, a tree with `r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"]` splits and `r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"] + 1` leaves (Figure 1).

```{r tree plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.2, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Pruned tree (per node: predicted class, churn probability, share of training customers)."}
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
```

The tree first splits on contract type, the most important variable (`r var_importance["Contract"]`% of importance), followed by tenure (`r var_importance["tenure"]`%) and total charges (`r var_importance["TotalCharges"]`%; Appendix A, Table A1). Customers with a contract of at least one year (40% of all customers) are fairly safe: only 10% of them churn. Month-to-month customers (60% of all customers) are much more likely to leave: 55% of them churn. Within this group, the type of internet matters most. Month-to-month fibre-optic customers (35% of all customers) churn at 67%. Those with less than 16 months' tenure are the riskiest group (18% of all customers): 81% of them churn. Among fibre customers who stay longer, price matters: 62% of those paying at least \$96 a month churn. Month-to-month customers with DSL or no internet (25% of all customers) churn at 38%, and tenure matters most: after six months, only 28% churn. Of newer customers without online backup, 63% churn.

On the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test customers, the tree predicts churn correctly in `r pct(acc_test)` of cases. This is well above the `r pct(acc_baseline)` baseline and close to the `r pct(acc_train)` on the training data, so the tree does not overfit; the unpruned tree only reaches `r pct(acc_full)`. Of the customers the tree flags as churners, `r pct(precision)` actually leave (precision), and it finds `r pct(recall)` of all churners (recall), giving an F1 score of `r sprintf("%.2f", f1)`.

# 5. Conclusions and Discussion

This report asked which customer characteristics are related to churn and which customers to target. Churn mainly depends on how strongly customers are tied to the provider through contract length, tenure, internet service and price. Customers with a long contract rarely churn, as switching is harder. New fibre customers churn most often. They pay for the most expensive service but are not yet loyal. Customers with extra services, such as online backup, seem more attached. The provider should therefore target month-to-month customers in their first year, especially fibre customers, e.g. with discounts on longer contracts, and promote extra services to new DSL customers. To improve the analysis, a lower cut-off could catch more of the `r pct(1 - recall)` missed churners, and satisfaction data could explain why customers leave.

# Appendix B

The code below reproduces all numbers, tables and figures in this report (R 4.3.3, `rpart` 4.1.23).

\begingroup
\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}

\begin{lstlisting}[
basicstyle=\ttfamily\fontsize{6}{6.4}\selectfont,
columns=fullflexible,
breaklines=true,
breakatwhitespace=false,
keepspaces=true,

frame=none
]
# 1. Packages: rpart fits CART trees, rpart.plot draws them
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

# 2. Load the data (data frame `data`: 4,000 customers, 13 variables)
setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%

# Descriptive statistics
str(data)                                                    # variable types: 3 numeric, 10 factors
summary(data)                                                # numeric: min, quartiles, mean, max; factors: counts
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Churn)), 1)                # churn rate in %
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Contract)), 1)             # contract types in %
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$Contract, data$Churn), 1), 1)        # churn rate per contract type
round(100 * prop.table(table(data$InternetService, data$Churn), 1), 1) # churn rate per internet service

# 3. Stratified 70/30 split: 70% of the churners and 70% of the non-churners go to the
#    training set, so both sets keep the 37.5% churn rate; the seed makes it reproducible
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]                          # 2,800 training customers
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]                         # remaining 1,200 test customers

# 4. Grow the full tree: cp = 0 switches off pruning, xval = 10 stores the
#    10-fold cross-validated error (xerror) for every cp value
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)

# 5. Tune cp with the 1-SE rule: smallest tree whose CV error is within
#    one standard error (xstd) of the minimum CV error
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]

# 6. Prune the full tree back to the chosen cp and compute variable importance
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %

# 7. Predict the test set (majority class of the leaf, cut-off 0.5) and evaluate
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

precision <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix["Yes", ]) # predicted churners that really churn
recall    <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # actual churners that are detected
f1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)          # harmonic mean of precision and recall
precision; recall; f1

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

# 8. Figure 1: the pruned tree
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)

# 9. Appendix A, Table A1: variable importance
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(var_importance),
                        `Importance (%)` = var_importance, check.names = FALSE),
             format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
\end{lstlisting}
